entries.8a6f90122a165573aeab2cda2813f16afe7640ce: <div sID="gen25000" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Mark.15" sID="Mark.15"/> <div eID="gen25000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25001" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25002" type="x-p"/> What we read of the sufferings of Christ, in the foregoing chapter, was but the prologue or introduction; here we have the completing of them. We left him condemned by the chief priests; but they could only show their teeth, they could not bite. Here we have him, I. Arraigned and accused before Pilate the Roman governor, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.1-Mark.15.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Cried out against by the common people, at the instigation of the priests, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.6-Mark.15.14">ver. 6-14</reference>. III. Condemned to be crucified immediately, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.15">ver. 15</reference>. IV. Bantered and abused, as a mock-king, by the Roman soldiers, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.16-Mark.15.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. V. Led out to the place of execution with all possible ignominy and disgrace, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.20-Mark.15.24">ver. 20-24</reference>. VI. Nailed to the cross between two thieves, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.25-Mark.15.28">ver. 25-28</reference>. VII. Reviled and abused by all that passed by, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.29-Mark.15.32">ver. 29-32</reference>. VIII. Forsaken for a time by his father, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.33-Mark.15.36">ver. 33-36</reference>. IX. Dying, and rending the veil, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.37-Mark.15.38">ver. 37, 38</reference>. X. Attested and witnessed to by the centurion and others, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.39-Mark.15.41">ver. 39-41</reference>. XI. Buried in the sepulchre of Joseph of Arimathea, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.42-Mark.15.47">ver. 42-47</reference>.
entries.c9dde5fada8af6b5f8801662375f09b3dc2eb201: <div eID="gen25002" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25001" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Brought before Pilate.</title> <div sID="gen25003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And straightway in the morning the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council, and bound Jesus, and carried <hi type="italic">him</hi> away, and delivered <hi type="italic">him</hi> to Pilate. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Pilate asked him, Art thou the King of the Jews? And he answering said unto him, Thou sayest <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> And the chief priests accused him of many things: but he answered nothing. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Pilate asked him again, saying, Answerest thou nothing? behold how many things they witness against thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> But Jesus yet answered nothing; so that Pilate marvelled. <hi type="super">6</hi> Now at <hi type="italic">that</hi> feast he released unto them one prisoner, whomsoever they desired. <hi type="super">7</hi> And there was <hi type="italic">one</hi> named Barabbas, <hi type="italic">which lay</hi> bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the multitude crying aloud began to desire <hi type="italic">him to do</hi> as he had ever done unto them. 9 But Pilate answered them, saying, Will ye that I release unto you the King of the Jews? <hi type="super">10</hi> For he knew that the chief priests had delivered him for envy. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the chief priests moved the people, that he should rather release Barabbas unto them. 12 And Pilate answered and said again unto them, What will ye then that I shall do <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> whom ye call the King of the Jews? <hi type="super">13</hi> And they cried out again, Crucify him. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then Pilate said unto them, Why, what evil hath he done? And they cried out the more exceedingly, Crucify him. <div eID="gen25003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25004" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. A <hi type="italic">consultation</hi> held by the great Sanhedrim for the effectual prosecution of our Lord Jesus. They met <hi type="italic">early in the morning</hi> about it, and went into a grand committee, to find out <hi type="italic">ways and means</hi> to get him put to death; they lost no time, but followed their blow in good earnest, lest there should be an <hi type="italic">uproar among the people.</hi> The unwearied industry of wicked people in doing that which is evil, should shame us for our backwardness and slothfulness in that which is good. They that <hi type="italic">war</hi> against Christ and thy soul, are up early; <hi type="italic">How long then wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?</hi> <div eID="gen25004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25005" type="x-p"/> II. The delivering of him up a prisoner to Pilate; they <hi type="italic">bound him.</hi> He was to be the great sacrifice, and sacrifices must be bound with cords, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.27">Ps. cxviii. 27</reference>. Christ was bound, to make bonds easy to us, and enable us, as Paul and Silas, to sing in bonds. It is good for us often to <hi type="italic">remember the bonds</hi> of the Lord Jesus, as bound with him who was <hi type="italic">bound for us.</hi> They led him through the streets of Jerusalem, to expose <hi type="italic">him</hi> to contempt, who, while he taught in the temple, but a day or two before, was had in veneration; and we may well imagine how miserably he looked after such a night's usage as he had had; so buffeted, spit upon, and abused. Their delivering him to the Roman power was a type of ruin of their church, which hereby they merited, and brought upon themselves; it signified that the promise, the covenant, and the oracles, of God, and the visible state church, which were the glory of Israel, and had been so long in their possession, should now be delivered up to the Gentiles. By delivering up the <hi type="italic">king</hi> they do, in effect, deliver up the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God,</hi> which is therefore, as it were, by their own consent, taken from them, and given to another nation. If they had delivered up Christ, to gratify the desires of the Romans, or to satisfy and jealousies of theirs concerning him, it had been another matter; but they voluntarily betrayed him that was <hi type="italic">Israel's crown,</hi> to them that were <hi type="italic">Israel's yoke.</hi> <div eID="gen25005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25006" type="x-p"/> III. The examining of him by Pilate upon interrogatories (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.2">v. 2</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews?</hi> Dost thou pretend to be so, to be that Messiah whom the Jews expect as a temporal prince?"—"Yea," saith Christ, "it is as <hi type="italic">thou sayest,</hi> I am that Messiah, but not such a one as they expect." He is the king that rules and protects his Israel according to the spirit, who are Jews inwardly by the circumcision of the spirit, and the king that will restrain and punish the carnal Jews, who continue in unbelief. <div eID="gen25006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25007" type="x-p"/> IV. The articles of impeachment exhibited against him, and his silence under the charge and accusation. The chief priests forgot the dignity of their place, when they turned informers, and did in person <hi type="italic">accuse Christ of many things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.3">v. 3</reference>), and witness against him, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.4">v. 4</reference>. Many of the Old-Testament prophets charge the priests of their times with great wickedness, in which <hi type="italic">well did they prophesy</hi> of these priests; see <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.26 Hos.5.1 Hos.6.9">Ezek. xxii. 26; Hos. v. 1; vi. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mic. iii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.4">Zeph. iii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.1.6">Mal. i. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.2.8">ii. 8</reference>. The destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans is said to be for the <hi type="italic">iniquity of the priests that shed the blood of the just,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.13">Lam. iv. 13</reference>. Note, Wicked priests are generally the worst of men. The better any thing is, the worse it is when it is corrupted. Lay persecutors have been generally found more compassionate than ecclesiastics. These priests were very eager and noisy in their accusation; but Christ <hi type="italic">answered nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.3">v. 3</reference>. When Pilate urged him to clear himself, and was desirous he should (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.4">v. 4</reference>), yet still he stood mute (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.5">v. 5</reference>), he <hi type="italic">answered nothing,</hi> which Pilate thought very strange. He gave Pilate a direct answer (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.2">v. 2</reference>), but would not answer the prosecutors and witnesses, because the things they alleged, were notoriously false, and he knew Pilate himself was convinced they were so. Note, As Christ <hi type="italic">spoke</hi> to admiration, so he <hi type="italic">kept silence</hi> to admiration. <div eID="gen25007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25008" type="x-p"/> V. The proposal Pilate made to the people, to have Jesus released to them, since it was the custom of the feast to grace the solemnity with the release of one prisoner. The people expected and demanded that he should do <hi type="italic">as he had ever done to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.8">v. 8</reference>); it was not an ill usage, but they would have it kept up. Now Pilate perceived that the chief priests delivered up Jesus <hi type="italic">for envy,</hi> because he had got such a reputation among the people as eclipsed theirs, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.10">v. 10</reference>. It was easy to see, comparing the eagerness of the prosecutors with the slenderness of the proofs, that it was not his <hi type="italic">guilt,</hi> but his <hi type="italic">goodness,</hi> not any thing <hi type="italic">mischievous</hi> or <hi type="italic">scandalous,</hi> but something <hi type="italic">meritorious</hi> and <hi type="italic">glorious,</hi> that they were provoked at. And therefore, hearing how much he was the darling of the crowd, he thought that he might safely appeal from the priests to the people, and that they would be proud of rescuing him out of the priests' hands; and he proposed an expedient for their doing it without danger of an <hi type="italic">uproar;</hi> let them demand him to be <hi type="italic">released,</hi> and Pilate will be ready to do it, and stop the mouths of the priests with this—that the people insisted upon his release. There was indeed another prisoner, <hi type="italic">one Barabbas,</hi> that had an interest, and would have some votes; but he questioned not but Jesus would out-poll him. <div eID="gen25008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25009" type="x-p"/> VI. The unanimous outrageous clamours of the people have <hi type="italic">Christ put to death,</hi> and particularly to have him <hi type="italic">crucified.</hi> It was a great surprise to Pilate, when he found the people so much under the influence of the priests, that they all agreed to desire that Barabbas might be <hi type="italic">released,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.11">v. 11</reference>. Pilate opposed it all he could; "<hi type="italic">What will ye that I shall do to him whom ye call the King of the Jews?</hi> Would not ye then have him released too?" <reference osisRef="Mark.15.12">v. 12</reference>. No, say they, <hi type="italic">Crucify him.</hi> The priests having put that in their mouths, the insist upon it; when Pilate objected, <hi type="italic">Why, what evil has he done?</hi> (a very material question in such a case), they did not pretend to answer it, but <hi type="italic">cried out more exceedingly,</hi> as they were more and more instigated and irritated by the priests, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him.</hi> Now the priests, who were very busy dispersing themselves and their creatures among the mob, to keep up the cry, promised themselves that it would influence Pilate two ways to condemn him. 1. It might incline him to believe Christ <hi type="italic">guilty,</hi> when there was so general an out-cry against him. "Surely," might Pilate think, "he must needs be a bad man, whom all the world is weary of." He would now conclude that he had been <hi type="italic">misinformed,</hi> when he was told what an interest he had in the people, and that the matter was not so. But the priest had hurried on the prosecution with so much expedition, that we may suppose that they who were Christ's friends, and would have opposed this cry, were at the other end of the town, and knew nothing of the matter. Note, It has been the common artifice of Satan, to put Christ and his religion into an ill name, and so to run them down. When once this sect, as they called it, comes to be <hi type="italic">every where spoken against,</hi> though <hi type="italic">without cause,</hi> then that is looked upon as <hi type="italic">cause enough</hi> to condemn it. But let us <hi type="italic">judge</hi> of persons and things by their merits, and the standard of God's word, and not prejudge by common fame and the cry of the country. 2. It might induce him to condemn Christ, to <hi type="italic">please</hi> the people, and indeed for <hi type="italic">fear of displeasing</hi> them. Though he was not so <hi type="italic">weak</hi> as to be governed by their opinion, to believe him guilty, yet he was so <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> as to be swayed by their outrage, to condemn him, though he believed him innocent; induced thereunto by reasons of state, and the wisdom of the world. Our Lord Jesus dying as a <hi type="italic">sacrifice</hi> for the <hi type="italic">sins of many,</hi> he fell a sacrifice to the <hi type="italic">rage of many.</hi>
entries.8779a0252654f1fca15a72464b8f6c02a895a39c: <div eID="gen25009" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Insulted and Condemned.</title> <div sID="gen25010" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And <hi type="italic">so</hi> Pilate, willing to content the people, released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged <hi type="italic">him,</hi> to be crucified. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the soldiers led him away into the hall, called Prætorium; and they call together the whole band. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they clothed him with purple, and platted a crown of thorns, and put it about his <hi type="italic">head,</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> And began to salute him, Hail, King of the Jews! <hi type="super">19</hi> And they smote him on the head with a reed, and did spit upon him, and bowing <hi type="italic">their</hi> knees worshipped him. <hi type="super">20</hi> And when they had mocked him, they took off the purple from him, and put his own clothes on him, and led him out to crucify him. 21 And they compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to bear his cross. <div eID="gen25010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25011" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Pilate, to gratify the Jews' malice, delivers Christ to be <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.15">v. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Willing to content the people,</hi> to <hi type="italic">do enough</hi> for them (so the word is), and make them easy, that he might keep them quiet, he <hi type="italic">released Barabbas unto them,</hi> who was the scandal and plague of their nation, and <hi type="italic">delivered Jesus</hi> to be <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> who was the glory and blessing of their nation. Though he <hi type="italic">had scourged him</hi> before, hoping that would <hi type="italic">content</hi> them, and then not designing to crucify him, yet he went on to that; for no wonder that he who could persuade himself to <hi type="italic">chastise</hi> one that was innocent (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.16">Luke xxiii. 16</reference>), could by degrees persuade himself to <hi type="italic">crucify</hi> him. <div eID="gen25011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25012" type="x-p"/> Christ was <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> for that was, 1. A <hi type="italic">bloody</hi> death, and <hi type="italic">without blood no remission,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.22">Heb. ix. 22</reference>. The blood is <hi type="italic">the life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen. ix. 4</reference>); it is the <hi type="italic">vehicle</hi> of the <hi type="italic">animal</hi> spirits, which <hi type="italic">connect</hi> the soul and body, so that the exhausting of the blood is the exhausting of the life. Christ was to lay down <hi type="italic">his life</hi> for us, and therefore <hi type="italic">shed his blood.</hi> Blood <hi type="italic">made atonement for the soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.11">Lev. xvii. 11</reference>), and therefore in every sacrifice of propitiation special order was given for the <hi type="italic">pouring out</hi> of the blood, and the <hi type="italic">sprinkling</hi> of that before the Lord. Now, that Christ might answer all these types, he <hi type="italic">shed his blood.</hi> 2. It was a <hi type="italic">painful</hi> death; the pains were exquisite and acute, for death made its assaults upon the vitals by the exterior parts, which are <hi type="italic">quickest of sense.</hi> Christ died, so as that he might <hi type="italic">feel himself die,</hi> because he was to be both the priest and the sacrifice; so that he might be <hi type="italic">active</hi> in dying; because he was to <hi type="italic">make his soul an offering</hi> for sin. Tully calls crucifixion, <hi type="italic">Teterrimum supplicium—A most tremendous punishment:</hi> Christ would meet death in its greatest terror, and so conquer it. 3. It was a <hi type="italic">shameful</hi> death, the death of slaves, and the vilest malefactors; so it was accounted among the Romans. The <hi type="italic">cross</hi> and the <hi type="italic">shame</hi> are put together. God having been injured in his honour by the sin of man, it is <hi type="italic">in his honour</hi> that Christ makes him <hi type="italic">satisfaction,</hi> not only by denying himself in, and divesting himself of, the honours due to his divine nature, for a time, but by submitting the greatest reproach and ignominy the human nature was capable of being loaded with. Yet this was not the worst. 4. It was a <hi type="italic">cursed</hi> death; thus it was branded by the Jewish law (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.23">Deut. xxi. 23</reference>); <hi type="italic">He that is hanged, is accursed of God,</hi> is under a particular mark of God's displeasure. It was the death that Saul's sons were put to, when the guilt of their father' bloody house was to be expiated, <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.6">2 Sam. xxi. 6</reference>. Haman and his sons were <hi type="italic">hanged,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.7.10">Esth. vii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.9.13">ix. 13</reference>. We do not read any of the prophets of the Old Testament that were <hi type="italic">hanged;</hi> but now that Christ has submitted to be <hi type="italic">hanged upon a tree,</hi> the reproach and curse of that kind of death are quite rolled away, so that it ought to be any hindrance to the comfort of those who die either innocently or penitently, nor any diminution from, but rather an addition to, the glory of those who die martyrs for Christ, to be as he was, hanged upon a tree. <div eID="gen25012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25013" type="x-p"/> II. Pilate, to gratify the gay humour of the Roman soldiers, delivered him to them, to be abused and spitefully treated, while they were preparing for the execution. They called together <hi type="italic">the whole regiment</hi> that was then in waiting, and they went into an inner hall, where they ignominiously abused our Lord Jesus, as a king, just as in the high priest's hall his servants had ignominiously abused him as a Prophet and Saviour. 1. Do kings wear robes of purple or scarlet? They <hi type="italic">clothed him with purple.</hi> This abuse done to Christ in his apparel should be an intimation to Christians, not to make the putting on of apparel <hi type="italic">their adorning,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1 Pet. iii. 4</reference>. Shall a purple or scarlet robe be matter of pride to a Christian, which was matter of reproach and shame to Christ. 2. Do kings wear <hi type="italic">crowns?</hi> They <hi type="italic">platted a crown of thorns,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put it on his head.</hi> A crown of straw, or rushes, would have been banter enough; but this was pain also. He wore the crown of thorns which we had deserved, that we might wear the crown of glory which he merited. Let us be <hi type="italic">taught</hi> by these <hi type="italic">thorns,</hi> as Gideon taught the men of Succoth, to hate sin, and be uneasy under it, and to be in love with Jesus Christ, who is here a lily among thorns. If we be at any time afflicted with a <hi type="italic">thorn in the flesh,</hi> let it be our comfort, that our high priest is touched with the feelings of our infirmities, having himself known what <hi type="italic">thorns in the flesh</hi> meant. 3. Are kings attended with the acclamations of their subjects, <hi type="italic">O king, live for ever?</hi> That also is mimicked; they saluted him with "<hi type="italic">Hail, King of the Jews;</hi> such a prince, and such a people, even good enough for one another." 4. Kings have <hi type="italic">sceptres</hi> put into their hand, marks of dominion, as the crown is of dignity; to imitate this, they put a <hi type="italic">reed in his right hand.</hi> Those that despise the authority of Jesus Christ, as not to be observed and obeyed, who regard not either the precepts of his word, or the threatenings of his wrath, do, in effect, <hi type="italic">put a reed in his hand;</hi> nay, and, as these here, <hi type="italic">smite him on the head</hi> with it, such is the indignity they do him. 5. Subjects, when they swear allegiance, were wont to <hi type="italic">kiss</hi> their sovereign; and this they offered to do, but, instead of that, <hi type="italic">spit upon him.</hi> 6. Kings used to be addressed upon the <hi type="italic">knee;</hi> and this also they brought into the jest, they <hi type="italic">bowed the knee, and worshipped him;</hi> this they did in scorn, to make themselves and one another laugh. We were by sin become liable to <hi type="italic">everlasting shame and contempt,</hi> to deliver us from which, our Lord Jesus submitted to this shame and contempt for us. He was thus mocked, not in <hi type="italic">his own clothes,</hi> but in another's, to signify that he suffered not for his own sin; the crime was ours, the shame his. Those who pretend subjection to Christ, but at the same time give themselves up to the service of the world and the flesh, do, in effect, the same that they did, who bowed the knee to him in mockery, and abused him with, <hi type="italic">Hail, king of the Jews,</hi> when they said, <hi type="italic">We have no king but Cæsar.</hi> Those that bow the knee to Christ, but do not bow the soul, that <hi type="italic">draw nigh to him with their mouths,</hi> and <hi type="italic">honour him with their lips,</hi> but <hi type="italic">their hearts are far from him,</hi> put the same affront upon him that these here did. <div eID="gen25013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25014" type="x-p"/> III. The soldiers, at the hour appointed, led him away from Pilate's judgment-hall to the place of execution (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.20">v. 20</reference>), as a sheep to the slaughter; he was <hi type="italic">led forth with the workers of iniquity,</hi> though he did no sin. But lest his death, under the load of his cross, which he was to carry, should prevent the further cruelties they intended, they compelled one Simon of Cyrene to carry his cross for him. He <hi type="italic">passed by, coming out of the country</hi> or out of the <hi type="italic">fields,</hi> not thinking of any such matter. Note, We must not think it strange, if crosses come upon us suddenly, and we be surprised by them. The cross was a very troublesome unwieldy load: but he that carried it a few minutes, had the honour to have his name upon the record in the book of God, though otherwise an obscure person; so that, wherever this gospel is preached; so that, wherever this gospel is preached, there shall this be told for a memorial to him: in like manner, though <hi type="italic">no affliction,</hi> no cross, <hi type="italic">for the present, be joyous, but grievous,</hi> yet afterward it yields a crown of glory to them that are exercised thereby.
entries.d870789916cb8528254f6015d46c2ae7480290eb: <div eID="gen25014" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crucifixion.</title> <div sID="gen25015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And they bring him unto the place Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, The place of a skull. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they gave him to drink wine mingled with myrrh: but he received <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <hi type="super">24</hi> And when they had crucified him, they parted his garments, casting lots upon them, what every man should take. <hi type="super">25</hi> And it was the third hour, and they crucified him. 26 And the superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS. <hi type="super">27</hi> And with him they crucify two thieves; the one on his right hand, and the other on his left. 28 And the scripture was fulfilled, which saith, And he was numbered with the transgressors. <hi type="super">29</hi> And they that passed by railed on him, wagging their heads, and saying, Ah, thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest <hi type="italic">it</hi> in three days, <hi type="super">30</hi> Save thyself, and come down from the cross. <hi type="super">31</hi> Likewise also the chief priests mocking said among themselves with the scribes, He saved others; himself he cannot save. <hi type="super">32</hi> Let Christ the King of Israel descend now from the cross, that we may see and believe. And they that were crucified with him reviled him. <div eID="gen25015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25016" type="x-p"/> We have here the <hi type="italic">crucifixion</hi> of our Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen25016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25017" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">place where</hi> he was crucified; it was called <hi type="italic">Golgotha—the place of a scull:</hi> some think, because of the heads of malefactors that were there cut off: it was the common place of execution, as Tyburn, for he was in all respects numbered with the transgressors. I know not how to give any credit to it, but divers of the ancients mention it as a current tradition, that in this place our first father Adam was buried, and they think it highly congruous that there Christ should be crucified; for as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive. Tertullian, Origen, Chrysostom, and Epiphanius (great names), take notice of it; nay, Cyprian adds, <hi type="italic">Creditur &#224; piis—Many good people believe</hi> that the blood of Christ crucified did trickle down upon the scull of Adam, who was buried in the same place. Something more credible is the tradition, that this mount Calvary was <hi type="italic">that mountain in the land of Moriah</hi> (and in the land of Moriah it certainly was, for so the country about Jerusalem was called), on which Isaac was to be offered; and the ram was offered instead of him; and then Abraham had an eye to <hi type="italic">this day</hi> of Christ, when he called the place <hi type="italic">Jehovah-jireh—The Lord will provide,</hi> expecting that so it would be seen in the <hi type="italic">mount of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen25017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25018" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">time when</hi> he was crucified; it was the <hi type="italic">third hour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.25">v. 25</reference>. He was brought before Pilate about the sixth hour (<reference osisRef="John.19.14">John xix. 14</reference>), according to the Roman way of reckoning, which John uses, with which ours at this day agrees, that is at six o'clock in the morning; and then, at the <hi type="italic">third hour,</hi> according to the Jews' way of reckoning, that is, about nine of the clock in the morning, or soon after, they nailed him to the cross. Dr. Lightfoot thinks the <hi type="italic">third hour</hi> is here mentioned, to intimate an aggravation of the wickedness of the priests, they were here prosecuting Christ to the death, though it was after the <hi type="italic">third hour,</hi> when they ought to have been attending the service of the temple, and offering the peace-offerings; it being the first day of the <hi type="italic">feast of unleavened bread,</hi> when there was to be a <hi type="italic">holy convocation.</hi> At that very time, when they should have been, according to the duty of their place, presiding in the public devotions, were they here venting their malice against the Lord Jesus; yet these were the men that seemed so zealous for the temple, and condemned Christ for speaking against it. Note, There are many who pretend to be <hi type="italic">for the church,</hi> who yet care not how seldom they <hi type="italic">go to church.</hi> <div eID="gen25018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25019" type="x-p"/> III. The indignities that were done him, when he was nailed to the cross; as if that had not been ignominious enough, they added several things to the ignominy of it. <div eID="gen25019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25020" type="x-p"/> 1. It being the custom to give <hi type="italic">wine</hi> to persons that were to be <hi type="italic">put to death,</hi> they <hi type="italic">mingled</hi> his with <hi type="italic">myrrh,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">bitter,</hi> and made it <hi type="italic">nauseous;</hi> he <hi type="italic">tasted</hi> it, but would not drink it; was willing to admit the bitterness of it, but not the benefit of it. <div eID="gen25020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25021" type="x-p"/> 2. The garments of those that were crucified, being, as with us, the executioners' fee, the soldiers <hi type="italic">cast lots</hi> upon his garments (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.24">v. 24</reference>), threw dice (as our soldiers do upon a drum-head), for them: so making themselves merry with his misery, and sitting at their sport while he was hanging in pain. <div eID="gen25021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25022" type="x-p"/> 3. They set up a superscription over his head, by which they intended to reproach him, but really did him both justice and honour, <hi type="italic">The king of the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.26">v. 26</reference>. Here was no crime alleged, but his sovereignty owned. Perhaps Pilate meant to cast disgrace upon Christ as a baffled king, or upon the Jews, who by their importunity had forced him, against his conscience, to condemn Christ, as a people that deserved no better a king than he seemed to be: however, God intended it to be the proclaiming even of Christ upon the cross, the <hi type="italic">king of Israel;</hi> though Pilate know not what he wrote, any more than Caiaphas what he said, <reference osisRef="John.11.51">John xi. 51</reference>. Christ crucified is king of his church, his spiritual Israel; and even then when he hung on the cross, he was like a king, <hi type="italic">conquering</hi> his and his people's enemies, and <hi type="italic">triumphing</hi> over them, <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>. Now he was writing his laws in his own blood, and preparing his favours for his subjects. Whenever we look unto Christ crucified, we must remember the inscription over his head, that he is a king, and we must give up ourselves to be his subjects, as Israelites indeed. <div eID="gen25022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25023" type="x-p"/> 4. They crucified <hi type="italic">two thieves</hi> with him, <hi type="italic">one on his right hand, the other on his left,</hi> and him in the midst as the worst of the three (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.27">v. 27</reference>); so great a degree of dishonour did they hereby intend him. And, no doubt, it gave him <hi type="italic">disturbance</hi> too. Some that have been imprisoned in the common gaols, for the testimony of Jesus, have complained of the company of cursing, swearing prisoners, more than any other of the grievances of their prison. Now, in the midst of such our Lord Jesus was <hi type="italic">crucified;</hi> while he lived he had, and there was occasion, <hi type="italic">associated</hi> with sinners, to do them good; and now when he died, he was for the same purpose joined with them, for he <hi type="italic">came into the world,</hi> and went out of it, to <hi type="italic">save sinners,</hi> even the chief. But this evangelist takes particular notice of the fulfilling of the scriptures in it, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.28">v. 28</reference>. In that famous prediction of Christ's sufferings (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>), it was foretold that he should be numbered with the <hi type="italic">transgressors,</hi> because he was made <hi type="italic">sin for us.</hi> <div eID="gen25023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25024" type="x-p"/> 5. The spectators, that is, the generality of them, instead of condoling with him in his misery, added to it by insulting over him. Surely never was such an instance of barbarous inhumanity toward the vilest malefactor: but thus the devil showed the utmost rage against him, and thus he submitted to the greatest dishonours that could be done him. <div eID="gen25024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25025" type="x-p"/> (1.) Even they that <hi type="italic">passed by,</hi> that were no way concerned, <hi type="italic">railed on him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.29">v. 29</reference>. If their hearts were so hardened, that their compassions were not moved with such a spectacle, yet they should have thought it enough to have their curiosity gratified; but that will not serve: as if they were not only divested of all humanity, but were devils in human shape, they taunted him, and expressed themselves with the utmost detestation of him, and indignation at him, and shot thick at him their arrows, even <hi type="italic">bitter words.</hi> The chief priests, no doubt, put these sarcasms into their mouths, <hi type="italic">Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, now,</hi> if thou canst, <hi type="italic">save thyself,</hi> and <hi type="italic">come down from the cross.</hi> They triumph as if now that they had got him to the cross, there were no danger of his <hi type="italic">destroying the temple;</hi> whereas the <hi type="italic">temple</hi> of which <hi type="italic">he</hi> spoke, he was now <hi type="italic">destroying,</hi> and did within <hi type="italic">three days build it up;</hi> and the temple of which <hi type="italic">they</hi> spoke, he did by men, that were <hi type="italic">his sword</hi> and <hi type="italic">his hand,</hi> destroy not many years after. When secure sinners think the danger is over, it is then most ready to seize them: the day of the Lord <hi type="italic">comes as a thief</hi> upon those that <hi type="italic">deny</hi> his coming, and say, Where is the promise of it? much more upon those that <hi type="italic">defy</hi> his coming, and say, <hi type="italic">Let him make speed, and hasten his work.</hi> <div eID="gen25025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25026" type="x-p"/> (2.) Even the chief priests, who, being <hi type="italic">taken from among men</hi> and ordained for men, should have compassion even on those that are out of the way, should be tender of those that are suffering and dying (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.1-Heb.5.2">Heb. v. 1, 2</reference>), yet they poured vinegar instead of oil into his wounds, they <hi type="italic">talked to the grief</hi> of him <hi type="italic">whom God had smitten</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>), they <hi type="italic">mocked him,</hi> they said, <hi type="italic">He saved others,</hi> healed and helped them, but now it appears that it was not by his own power, for <hi type="italic">himself he cannot save.</hi> They challenged him to <hi type="italic">come down from the cross,</hi> if he could, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.32">v. 32</reference>. Let them but <hi type="italic">see</hi> that, and they would <hi type="italic">believe;</hi> whereas they would not believe, when he gave them a more convincing sign than that, when he came up from the grave. These chief priests, one would think, might now have found themselves <hi type="italic">other work</hi> to do: if they would not go to do their duty in <hi type="italic">the temple,</hi> yet they might have been employed in an office not foreign to their profession; though they would not offer any counsel or comfort to the Lord Jesus, yet they might have given some help to the thieves in their dying moments (the monks and priests in Popish countries are very officious about criminals broken upon the wheel, a death much like that of the cross); but they do not think that their business. <div eID="gen25026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25027" type="x-p"/> (3.) Even they that were crucified with him, reviled him (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.32">v. 32</reference>); one of them did, so wretchedly was his heart hardened even in the depth of misery, and at the door of eternity.
entries.c27b4b3e7fe740f65a6f94eed6151985680fb83f: <div eID="gen25027" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crucifixion.</title> <div sID="gen25028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <hi type="super">34</hi> And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? <hi type="super">35</hi> And some of them that stood by, when they heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> said, Behold, he calleth Elias. <hi type="super">36</hi> And one ran and filled a sponge full of vinegar, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on a reed, and gave him to drink, saying, Let alone; let us see whether Elias will come to take him down. <hi type="super">37</hi> And Jesus cried with a loud voice, and gave up the ghost. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God. <hi type="super">40</hi> There were also women looking on afar off: among whom was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome; <hi type="super">41</hi> (Who also, when he was in Galilee, followed him, and ministered unto him;) and many other women which came up with him unto Jerusalem. <div eID="gen25028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25029" type="x-p"/> Here we have an account of Christ's dying, how his enemies abused him, and God honoured him at his death. <div eID="gen25029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25030" type="x-p"/> I. There was a thick <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> over <hi type="italic">the whole land</hi> (some think over the whole earth), for three hours, from noon till three of the clock. Now the scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Amos viii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will cause the sun to go down at noon,</hi> and I will <hi type="italic">darken the earth in the clear day;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Jer.15.9">Jer. xv. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Her sun is gone down while it is yet day.</hi> The Jews have often demanded of Christ a <hi type="italic">sign from heaven;</hi> and now they had one, but such a one as signified the blinding of their eyes. It was a sign of the darkness that was come, and coming, upon the Jewish church and nation. They were doing their utmost to extinguish the Sun of righteousness, which was now setting, and the rising again of which they would never own; and what then might be expected among them but a worse than Egyptian darkness? This intimated to them, that the things which belonged to their peace, were now <hi type="italic">hid from their eyes,</hi> and that the day of the Lord was at hand, which should be to them a <hi type="italic">day of darkness and gloominess,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.2.1-Joel.2.2">Joel ii. 1, 2</reference>. It was the power of darkness that they were now under, the works of darkness that they were now doing; and such as this should their doom justly be, who <hi type="italic">loved darkness rather than light.</hi> <div eID="gen25030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25031" type="x-p"/> II. Toward the close of this darkness, our Lord Jesus, in the agony of his soul, cried out, <hi type="italic">My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.34">v. 34</reference>. The darkness signified the present cloud which the human soul of Christ was under, when he was making it an <hi type="italic">offering for sin.</hi> Mr. Fox, in his <hi type="italic">Acts and Monuments</hi> (vol. 3, p. 160), tells of one Dr. Hunter, a martyr in queen Mary's time, who, being fastened to the stake, to be burnt, put up this short prayer, <hi type="italic">Son of God, shine upon me;</hi> and immediately the sun in the firmament shone out of the dark cloud, so full in his face, that he was forced to look another way, which was very comfortable to him. But our Lord Jesus, on the contrary, was denied the light of the sun, when he was in his sufferings, to signifying the withdrawing of the light of God's countenance. And this he complained of more than any thing; he did not complain of his disciples' forsaking him, but of his Father's, 1. Because this <hi type="italic">wounded his spirit;</hi> and that is a thing <hi type="italic">hard to bear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.14">Prov. xviii. 14</reference>); brought the waters into his soul, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1-Ps.69.3">Ps. lxix. 1-3</reference>. 2. Because in this especially he was <hi type="italic">made sin for us;</hi> our iniquities had deserved <hi type="italic">indignation and wrath</hi> upon the soul (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.8">Rom. ii. 8</reference>), and therefore, Christ, being made a <hi type="italic">sacrifice,</hi> underwent as much of it as he was capable of; and it could not but bear hard indeed upon him who had lain <hi type="italic">in the bosom</hi> of the Father from eternity, and was <hi type="italic">always his light.</hi> These symptoms of divine wrath, which Christ was under in his sufferings, were like that fire from heaven which had been sent sometimes, in extraordinary cases, to consume the sacrifices (as <reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Lev. ix. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2 Chron. vii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.38">1 Kings xviii. 38</reference>); and it was always a token of God's acceptance. The fire that should have fallen upon the <hi type="italic">sinner,</hi> if God had not been <hi type="italic">pacified,</hi> fell upon the <hi type="italic">sacrifice,</hi> as a token that he was so; therefore it now fell upon Christ, and extorted him from this <hi type="italic">loud</hi> and <hi type="italic">bitter</hi> cry. When Paul was to be <hi type="italic">offered</hi> as a sacrifice for the <hi type="italic">service of saints,</hi> he could <hi type="italic">joy</hi> and <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Phil. ii. 17</reference>); but it is another thing to be offered as a sacrifice for <hi type="italic">the sin of sinners.</hi> Now, at the <hi type="italic">sixth hour,</hi> and so to the <hi type="italic">ninth,</hi> the <hi type="italic">sun</hi> was <hi type="italic">darkened</hi> by an extraordinary eclipse; and if it be true, as some astronomers compute, that in the evening of this day on which Christ died there was an eclipse of the moon, that was natural and expected, in which seven digits of the moon were darkened, and it continued from five o'clock till seven, it is remarkable, and yet further significant of the darkness of the time that then was. When the <hi type="italic">sun</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">darkened,</hi> the <hi type="italic">moon</hi> also shall <hi type="italic">not give her light.</hi> <div eID="gen25031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25032" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's prayer was bantered by them that stood by (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.35-Mark.15.36">v. 35, 36</reference>); because he cried, <hi type="italic">Eli, Eli,</hi> or (as Mark has it, according to the Syriac dialect) <hi type="italic">Eloi, Eloi,</hi> they said, <hi type="italic">He calls for Elias,</hi> though they knew very well what he said, and what it signified, <hi type="italic">My God, My God.</hi> Thus did they represent him as <hi type="italic">praying to saints,</hi> either because he had abandoned God, or God had abandoned him; and hereby they would make him more and more odious to the people. One of them <hi type="italic">filled a sponge with vinegar,</hi> and reached it up to him upon a reed; "Let him cool his mouth with that, it is a drink good enough for him," <reference osisRef="Mark.15.36">v. 36</reference>. This was intended for a further affront and abuse to him; and whoever it was that checked him who did it, did but add to the reproach; "<hi type="italic">Let him alone;</hi> he has called for Elias: <hi type="italic">let us see whether Elias will come take him down;</hi> and if not, we may conclude that he also hath abandoned him." <div eID="gen25032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25033" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ did again <hi type="italic">cry with a loud voice,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">gave up the ghost,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.37">v. 37</reference>. He was now commending his soul into his Father's hand; and though God is not moved with any <hi type="italic">bodily exercise,</hi> yet this loud voice signified the great strength and ardency of affection wherewith he did it; to teach us, in every thing wherein we have to do with God, to put forth our utmost vigour, and to perform all the duties of religion, particularly that of <hi type="italic">self-resignation,</hi> with our whole heart and whole soul; and then, though speech fails, that we cannot <hi type="italic">cry with a loud voice,</hi> as Christ did, yet if God be the <hi type="italic">strength of the heart,</hi> that will not fail. Christ was really and truly <hi type="italic">dead,</hi> for he <hi type="italic">gave up the ghost;</hi> his human soul departed to the world of spirits, and left his body a breathless clod of clay. <div eID="gen25033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25034" type="x-p"/> V. Just at that instant that Christ died upon <hi type="italic">mount Calvary,</hi> the veil of the <hi type="italic">temple</hi> was <hi type="italic">rent in twain from the top to the bottom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.38">v. 38</reference>. This bespoke a great deal, 1. Of the terror of the unbelieving Jews; for it was a presage of the utter destruction of their church and nation, which followed not long after; it was like the cutting asunder of the <hi type="italic">staff of beauty</hi> (for this veil was exceedingly splendid and glorious, <reference osisRef="Exod.26.31">Exod. xxvi. 31</reference>), and that was done at the same time when they gave for his price <hi type="italic">thirty pieces of silver</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.10">Zech. xi. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">12</reference>), to <hi type="italic">break the covenant which he had made with that people.</hi> Now it was time to cry, <hi type="italic">Ichabod, The glory is departed from Israel.</hi> Some think that the story which Josephus relates, of the temple door opening of its own accord, with that voice, <hi type="italic">Let us depart hence,</hi> some years before the destruction of Jerusalem, is the same with this; but that is not probable: however, this had the same signification, according to that (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will tear, and go away.</hi> 2. It bespeaks a great deal of comfort to all believing Christians, for it signifies the consecrating and laying open to us of a <hi type="italic">new and living way into the holiest</hi> by the <hi type="italic">blood of Jesus.</hi> <div eID="gen25034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25035" type="x-p"/> VI. The centurion who commanded the detachment which had the oversight of the execution was convinced, and confessed that this Jesus was the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.39">v. 39</reference>. One thing that satisfied him, was, that he <hi type="italic">so cried out, and gave up the ghost:</hi> that one who was ready to give up the ghost, should be able to cry out so, was very surprising. Of all the sad spectacles of this kind he never observed the like; and that one who had strength to cry so loud, should yet immediately give up the ghost, this also made him wonder; and he said, to the honour of Christ, and the shame of those that abused him, <hi type="italic">Truly this man was the Son of God.</hi> But what reason had he to say so? I answer, 1. He had reason to say that he suffered <hi type="italic">unjustly,</hi> and had a great deal of wrong done him. Note, He suffered for saying that he was <hi type="italic">the Son of God;</hi> and it was true, he did say so, so that if he suffered unjustly, as it was plain by all the circumstances of his suffering that he did, then what he said was true, and he was indeed the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> 2. He had reason to say that he was a <hi type="italic">favourite of heaven,</hi> and one for whom the almighty power was particularly engaged, seeing how Heaven did him honour at his death, and frowned upon his persecutors. "Surely," thinks he, "this must be some divine person, highly beloved of God." This he expresses by such words as denote his eternal generation as God, and his special designation to the office of Mediator, though he meant not so. Our Lord Jesus, even in the depth of his sufferings and humiliation, was the Son of God, and was declared to be so <hi type="italic">with power.</hi> <div eID="gen25035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25036" type="x-p"/> VII. There were some of his friends, the good women especially, that attended him (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.40-Mark.15.41">v. 40, 41</reference>); <hi type="italic">There were women looking on afar off:</hi> the <hi type="italic">men</hi> durst not be seen at all, the mob was so very outrageous; <hi type="italic">Currenti cede furori—Give way to the raging torrent,</hi> they thought, was good counsel now. The women durst not come near, but stood at a distance, overwhelmed with grief. Some of these women are here named. <hi type="italic">Mary Magdalene</hi> was one; she had been his patient, and owed all her comfort to his power and goodness, which rescued her out of the possession of seven devils, in gratitude for which she thought she could never do enough for him. <hi type="italic">Mary</hi> also was there, <hi type="italic">the mother of James the little, Jacobus parvus,</hi> so the word is; probably, he was so called because he was, like Zaccheus, little of stature. This Mary was the wife of Cleophas or Alpheus, sister to the virgin Mary. These women had followed Christ <hi type="italic">from Galilee,</hi> though they were not required to attend the feast, as the males were; but it is probably that they came, in expectation that his temporal kingdom would now shortly be set up, and big with hopes of preferment for themselves, and their relations under him. It is plain that the mother of Zebedee's children was so (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.21">Matt. xx. 21</reference>); and now to see <hi type="italic">him</hi> upon a cross, whom they thought to have seen upon a throne, could not but be a great disappointment to them. Note, Those that follow Christ, in expectation of great things in this world by him, and by the profession of his religion, may probably live to see themselves sadly disappointed.
entries.54147cf02ef68140bff94c375125d14b8586f68c: <div eID="gen25036" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burial of Christ; The Women at the Sepulchre.</title> <div sID="gen25037" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">42</hi> And now when the even was come, because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath, <hi type="super">43</hi> Joseph of Arimathæa, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus. <hi type="super">44</hi> And Pilate marvelled if he were already dead: and calling <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> the centurion, he asked him whether he had been any while dead. <hi type="super">45</hi> And when he knew <hi type="italic">it</hi> of the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph. <hi type="super">46</hi> And he bought fine linen, and took him down, and wrapped him in the linen, and laid him in a sepulchre which was hewn out of a rock, and rolled a stone unto the door of the sepulchre. <hi type="super">47</hi> And Mary Magdalene and Mary <hi type="italic">the mother</hi> of Joses beheld where he was laid. <div eID="gen25037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25038" type="x-p"/> We are here attending the funeral of our Lord Jesus, a solemn, mournful funeral. O that we may by grace be planted in the likeness of it! Observe, <div eID="gen25038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25039" type="x-p"/> I. How the body of Christ was <hi type="italic">begged.</hi> It was, as the dead bodies of malefactors are, at the disposal of the government. Those that hurried him to the cross, designed that he should make <hi type="italic">his grave with the wicked;</hi> but God designed he should make it <hi type="italic">with the rich</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa. liii. 9</reference>), and so he did. We are here told, <div eID="gen25039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25040" type="x-p"/> 1. When the body of Christ was begged, in order to its being buried, and why such haste was made with the funeral; <hi type="italic">The even was come,</hi> and it was <hi type="italic">the preparation,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the day before the sabbath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.42">v. 42</reference>. The Jews were more strict in the observation of the sabbath than of any other feast; and therefore, though this day was itself a <hi type="italic">feast-day,</hi> yet they observed it more religiously as the <hi type="italic">eve</hi> of the <hi type="italic">sabbath;</hi> when they prepared their houses and tables for the <hi type="italic">splendid</hi> and <hi type="italic">joyful</hi> solemnizing of the sabbath day. Note, The day before the sabbath should be a day of preparation for the sabbath, not of our houses and tables, but of our hearts, which, as much as possible, should be <hi type="italic">freed</hi> from the cares and business of the world, and <hi type="italic">fixed,</hi> and put in frame for the service and enjoyment of God. Such work is to be done, and such advantages are to be gained on the sabbath day, that it is requisite we should get ready for it a day before; nay, the whole week should be divided between the improvement of the foregoing sabbath and the preparation for the following sabbath. <div eID="gen25040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25041" type="x-p"/> 2. Who was it that begged the body, and took care for the decent interment of it; it was <hi type="italic">Joseph of Arimathea,</hi> who is here called an <hi type="italic">honourable counsellor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.43">v. 43</reference>), a person of character and distinction, and in an office of public trust; some think <hi type="italic">in the state,</hi> and that he was one of Pilate's privy council; his post rather seems to have been <hi type="italic">in the church,</hi> he was one of the <hi type="italic">great Sanhedrim</hi> of the Jews, or one of the high priest's council. He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">euschemon bouleutes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a counsellor that conducted himself in his place as did become him.</hi> Those are truly honourable, and those only, in place of power and trust, who make conscience of their duty, and whose deportment is agreeable to their preferment. But here is a more shining character put upon him; he was one that <hi type="italic">waited for the kingdom of God,</hi> the kingdom of grace on earth, and of glory in heaven, the kingdom of the Messiah. Note, Those who <hi type="italic">wait for the kingdom of God,</hi> and hope for an interest in the privileges of it, must show it by their forwardness to own Christ's cause and interest, even then when it seems to be crushed and run down. Observe, Even among the <hi type="italic">honourable counsellors</hi> there were some, there was <hi type="italic">one</hi> at least, that waited for the kingdom of God, whose faith will condemn the unbelief of all the rest. This man God raised up for this necessary service, when none of Christ's disciples could, or durst, undertake it, having neither purse, nor interest, nor courage, for it. <hi type="italic">Joseph went in boldly to Pilate;</hi> though he knew how much it would affront the chief priests, who had loaded him with so much reproach, to see any honour done him, yet he <hi type="italic">put on courage;</hi> perhaps at first he was a little afraid, but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tolmesas</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">taking heart on it,</hi> he determined to show this respect to the remains of the Lord Jesus, let the worst come to the worst. <div eID="gen25041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25042" type="x-p"/> 3. What a surprise it was to Pilate, to hear that he was <hi type="italic">dead</hi> (Pilate, perhaps, expecting that he would have saved himself, and come down from the cross), especially that he was <hi type="italic">already dead,</hi> that one who seemed to have more than ordinary vigour, should so soon yield to death. Every circumstance of Christ's dying was marvellous; for from first to last his name was called <hi type="italic">Wonderful.</hi> Pilate doubted (so some understand it) whether he was yet dead or no, fearing lest he should be imposed upon, and the body should be <hi type="italic">taken down alive,</hi> and recovered, whereas the sentence was, as with us, to hang <hi type="italic">till the body be dead.</hi> He therefore called the centurion, his own officer, and asked him <hi type="italic">whether he had been any while dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.44">v. 44</reference>), whether it was so long since they perceived any sign of life in him, any breath or motion, that they might conclude he was dead past recall. The centurion could assure him of this, for he had particularly observed how <hi type="italic">he gave up the ghost,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.15.39">v. 39</reference>. There was a special providence in it, that Pilate should be so strict in examining this, that there might be no pretence to say that he was buried alive, and so to take away the truth of his resurrection; and so fully was this determined, that the objection was never started. Thus the truth of Christ gains confirmation, sometimes, even from its enemies. <div eID="gen25042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25043" type="x-p"/> II. How the body of Christ was <hi type="italic">buried.</hi> Pilate gave Joseph leave to take down the body, and do what he pleased with it. It was a wonder the chief priests were not too quick for him, and had not first begged the body of Pilate, to expose it and drag it about the streets, but that remainder of their wrath did God restrain, and gave that invaluable prize to Joseph, who knew how to value it; and the hearts of the priests were so influenced, that they did not oppose it. <hi type="italic">Sit divus, modo non sit vivus—We care not for his being adored, provided he be not revived.</hi> <div eID="gen25043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25044" type="x-p"/> 1. Joseph bought <hi type="italic">fine linen</hi> to wrap the body in, though in such a case old linen that had been worn might have been thought sufficient. In paying respects to Christ it becomes us to be <hi type="italic">generous,</hi> and to serve him with the <hi type="italic">best</hi> that can be got, not with that which can be got at the best hand. <div eID="gen25044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25045" type="x-p"/> 2. He <hi type="italic">took down</hi> the body, mangled and macerated as it was, and <hi type="italic">wrapt it in the linen</hi> as a treasure of great worth. Our Lord Jesus hath commanded himself to be delivered to us sacramentally in the ordinance of the Lord's supper, which we should receive in such a manner as may best express our love to him who loved us and died for us. <div eID="gen25045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25046" type="x-p"/> 3. He <hi type="italic">laid it in a sepulchre</hi> of his own, in a private place. We sometimes find it spoken of in the story of the kings of Judah, as a slur upon the memory of the wicked kings, that they were not buried in the <hi type="italic">sepulchres of the kings;</hi> our Lord Jesus, though he did no evil but much good, and to him was given the throne of his father David, yet was buried in the graves of the common people, for it was not in this world, but in the other, that <hi type="italic">his rest was glorious.</hi> The sepulchre belonged to Joseph. Abraham when he had no other possession in the land of Canaan, yet had a burying-place, but Christ had not so much as that. This sepulchre was <hi type="italic">hewn out of a rock,</hi> for Christ died to make the grave a <hi type="italic">refuge</hi> and shelter to the saints, and being hewn out of a rock, it is a <hi type="italic">strong</hi> refuge. <hi type="italic">O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave!</hi> Christ himself is a <hi type="italic">hiding place</hi> to his people, that is, as <hi type="italic">the shadow of a great rock.</hi> <div eID="gen25046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25047" type="x-p"/> 4. He <hi type="italic">rolled a stone to the door of the sepulchre,</hi> for so the manner of the Jews was to bury. When Daniel was put into the lion's den, a stone was laid to the mouth of it to keep him in, as here to the door of Christ's sepulchre, but neither of them could keep off the angels' visits to the prisoners. <div eID="gen25047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25048" type="x-p"/> 5. Some of the good women attended the funeral, and <hi type="italic">beheld where he was laid,</hi> that they might come after the sabbath to anoint the dead body, because they had not time to do it now. When Moses, the mediator and lawgiver of the Jewish church, was buried, care was taken that no man should <hi type="italic">know of his sepulchre</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.34.6">Deut. xxxiv. 6</reference>), because the respect of the people towards his person were to die with him; but when our great Mediator and Lawgiver was buried, special notice was taken of his sepulchre, because he was to <hi type="italic">rise again:</hi> and the care taken of his body, bespeaks the care which he himself will take concerning his body the church. Even when it seems to be a dead body, and as a valley full of dry bones, it shall be preserved in order to a resurrection; as shall also the dead bodies of the saints, with whose dust there is a covenant in force which shall not be forgotten. Our mediations on Christ's burial should lead us to think of our own, and should help to make the grave familiar to us, and so to render that bed easy which we must shortly make in the darkness. Frequent thoughts of it would not only take off the dread and terror of it, but quicken us, since the <hi type="italic">graves</hi> are always ready for us, to get ready for the graves, <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job xvii. 1</reference>.  <chapter eID="Mark.15"/> <div eID="gen25048" type="x-p"/>

entries.f6a025d5ac5144bd5ac57281aca439146290e9c2: <div eID="gen39674" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39675" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39676" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39676" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39675" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39677" type="x-p"/> Jesus is brought before Pilate, examined, and accused, but makes no answer, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.1-Mar.15.5">Mar 15:1-5</reference>. The multitude clamor for the release of Barabbas, and the crucifixion of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.6-Mar.15.14">Mar 15:6-14</reference>. Pilate consents, and he is led away, mocked, insulted, and nailed to the cross, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.15-Mar.15.26">Mar 15:15-26</reference>. Two thieves are crucified with him, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.27">Mar 15:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.28">Mar 15:28</reference>. While hanging on the cross, he is mocked and insulted, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.29-Mar.15.32">Mar 15:29-32</reference>. The miraculous darkness and our Lord's death, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.33-Mar.15.37">Mar 15:33-37</reference>. The rending of the veil, and the confession of the centurion, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.38">Mar 15:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.39">Mar 15:39</reference>. Several women attend and behold his death, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.40">Mar 15:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.41">Mar 15:41</reference>. Joseph of Arimathea begs the body from Pilate, and buries it, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.42-Mar.15.46">Mar 15:42-46</reference>. Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of Joses, note the place of his burial, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.47">Mar 15:47</reference>. <div eID="gen39677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39678" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39679" type="x-p"/> In the morning - See <reference osisRef="Mat.27.1">Mat 27:1</reference>, etc.
entries.22b8d64d1a26b0b761812f4a1938be8164efef22: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39680" type="x-p"/> The multitude crying aloud - Αναβοησας. The word itself strongly marks the vociferations, or, to come nearer the original word, the bellowing of the multitude. It signifies, properly, a loud and long cry, such as Christ emitted on the cross. See the whole history of these proceedings against our Lord treated at large, on Matthew 27 (note).
entries.c88889fa66a199899b96ab7d4d2e35822d8aa579: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen39680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39681" type="x-p"/> And platted a crown of thorns - In the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.29">Mat 27:29</reference> (note), I have ventured to express a doubt whether our Lord was crowned with thorns, in our sense of the word; this crown being designed as an instrument of torture. I am still of the same opinion, having considered the subject more closely since writing that note. As there I have referred to Bishop Pearce, a man whose merit as a commentator is far beyond my praise, and who, it is to be regretted, did not complete his work on the New Testament, I think it right to insert the whole of his note here. "The word ακανθων may as well be the plural genitive case of the word ακανθος as of ακανθη: if of the latter, it is rightly translated, of thorns; but the former would signify what we call bear's-foot, and the French, branche ursine. This is not of the thorny kind of plants, but is soft and smooth. Virgil calls it mollis acanthus, Ecl. iii. 45, Geor. iv. 137. So does Pliny, sec. Epist. ver. 6. And Pliny the elder, in his Nat. Hist. xxii. 22, p. 277, edit. Hard., says that it is laevis, smooth; and that it is one of those plants that are cultivated in gardens. I have somewhere read, but cannot at present recollect where, that this soft and smooth herb was very common in and about Jerusalem. I find nothing in the New Testament said concerning this crown, which Pilate's soldiers put on the head of Jesus, to incline one to think that it was of thorns, and intended, as is usually supposed, to put him to pain. The reed put into his hand, and the scarlet robe on his back, were only meant as marks of mockery and contempt. One may also reasonably judge, by the soldiers being said to plat this crown, that it was not composed of such twigs and leaves as were of a thorny nature. I do not find that it is mentioned by any of the primitive Christian writers as an instance of the cruelty used towards our Savior, before he was led to his crucifixion, till the time of Tertullian, who lived after Jesus's death at the distance of above 160 years. He indeed seems to have understood ακανθων in the sense of thorns, and says, De Corona Militar. sect. xiv. edit. Pamel. Franck. 1597, Quale, oro te, Jesus Christus sertum pro utroque sexu subiit? Ex spinis, opinor, et tribulis. The total silence of Polycarp, Barnabas, Clem. Romanus, and all the other Christian writers whose works are now extant, and who wrote before Tertullian, in particular, will give some weight to incline one to think that this crown was not platted with thorns. But as this is a point on which we have not sufficient evidence, I leave it almost in the same state of uncertainty in which I found it. The reader may see a satisfactory account of acanthus, bear's-foot, in Quincy's English Dispensatory, part ii. sect. 3, edit. 8, 1742." <div eID="gen39681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39682" type="x-p"/> This is the whole of the learned and judicious prelate's note; on which I have only to observed that the species of acanthus described by Virgil and the two Plinys, as mollis and laevis, soft and smooth, is, no doubt, the same as that formerly used in medicine, and described by Quincy and other pharmacopaeists; but there are other species of the same plant that are prickly, and particularly those called the acanthus spinosus, and the ilicifolius, the latter of which is common in both the Indies: this has leaves something like our common holly, the jagged edges of which are armed with prickles; but I do not conceive that this kind was used, nor indeed any other plant of a thorny nature, as the Roman soldiers who platted the crown could have no interest in adding to our Lord's sufferings; though they smote him with the rod, yet their chief object was to render him ridiculous, for pretending, as they imagined, to regal authority. The common wild acanthas or bear's-foot, which I have often met in the dry turf bogs in Ireland, though it have the appearance of being prickly, yet is not, in fact, so. Several shoots grow from one root, about four or five inches long, and about as thick as a little finger. A parcel of such branches, platted by their roots in a string, night be made to look even ornamental, tied about the temples and round the head. It would finely imitate a crown or diadem. But I know not if this plant be a native of Judea.
entries.bb3d07c00881cc39e3db506cea243ef6886098db: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39683" type="x-p"/> A Cyrenian - One of Cyrene, a celebrated city in the Pentapolis of Libya. <div eID="gen39683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39684" type="x-p"/> The father of Alexander and Rufus - It appears that these two persons were well known among the first disciples of our Lord. It is not unlikely that this is the same Alexander who is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Act.19.33">Act 19:33</reference>, and that the other is the Rufus spoken of by St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.13">Rom 16:13</reference>.
entries.72b7d64c51fd4904f375df21d0af60307a24a1f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen39684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39685" type="x-p"/> The third hour - It has been before observed, that the Jews divided their night into four watches, of three hours each. They also divided the day into four general parts. The first began at sunrise. The second three hours after. The third at mid-day. The fourth three hours after, and continued till sunset. Christ having been nailed to the cross a little after mid-day, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.14-Joh.19.16">Joh 19:14-16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.17">Joh 19:17</reference>, and having expired about three o'clock, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.33">Mar 15:33</reference>, the whole business of the crucifixion was finished within the space of this third division of the day, which Mark calls here the third hour. Commentators and critics have found it very difficult to reconcile this third hour of Mark, with the sixth hour of John, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.14">Joh 19:14</reference>. It is supposed that the true reading, in <reference osisRef="Joh.19.14">Joh 19:14</reference>, should be τριτη, the third, instead of ἑκτη the sixth; a mistake which might have readily taken place in ancient times, when the character γ gamma, which was put for τριτη, three, might have been mistaken for Ϛ episema, or sigma tau, which signifies six. And τριτη, the third, instead of ἑκτη, the sixth, is the reading of some very eminent MSS. in the place in question, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.14">Joh 19:14</reference>. See Bengel, Newcome, Macknight, Lightfoot, Rosenmuller, etc., on this perplexing point.
entries.cd6f4495fb85743b0c26913748d8dcfa54c98c58: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39686" type="x-p"/> Two thieves - A copy of the Itala tells their names: One on the right hand - named Zoathon; and one on the left hand - named Chammatha.
entries.7137c64935e41eea826e6b1a4dfb60b9f7901a71: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen39686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39687" type="x-p"/> The scripture was fulfilled - All this verse is wanting in many MSS., some versions, and several of the fathers.
entries.cc70f021593bb6f16fc5ac135a9c3adc2102aa6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen39687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39688" type="x-p"/> And believe - In him is added by DFGHPBHV, and upwards of sixty others; as also the Armenian, Slavonic, and four Itala.
entries.af6876b5a482314cacb3197439d161254e50ced5: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen39688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39689" type="x-p"/> My God, my God, etc. - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.46">Mat 27:46</reference> (note).
entries.e2627c3b64a17d4c2939b2b16c836b97d40ec4f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen39689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39690" type="x-p"/> Gave up the ghost - This was about three o'clock, or what was termed by the Jews the ninth hour; about the time that the paschal lamb was usually sacrificed. The darkness mentioned here must have endured about two hours and a half. Concerning this eclipse, see on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.45">Mat 27:45</reference> (note).
entries.712f41cb9341df4a3b2ee729622f38f9c05a2299: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen39690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39691" type="x-p"/> Joses - Some MSS. and versions read Joset, others Joseph. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.56">Mat 27:56</reference> (note).
entries.dda42ac060414e1b887e845745ebfe71c09cd05e: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen39691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39692" type="x-p"/> The day before the Sabbath - What we would call Friday evening. As the law of Moses had ordered that no criminal should continue hanging on a tree or gibbet till the setting of the sun, Joseph, fearing that the body of our Lord might be taken down, and thrown into the common grave with the two robbers, came and earnestly entreated Pilate to deliver it to him, that he might bury it in his own new tomb. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.27.56">Mat 27:56</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.60">Mat 27:60</reference> (note).
entries.b19c609fd263bf3631917bbc936068f95464d1eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen39692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39693" type="x-p"/> Went in boldly unto Pilate - He who was a coward before now acts a more open, fearless part, than any of the disciples of our Lord! This the Holy Spirit has thought worthy of especial notice. It needed no small measure of courage to declare now for Jesus, who had been a few hours ago condemned as a blasphemer by the Jews, and as a seditious person by the Romans; and this was the more remarkable in Joseph, because hitherto, for fear of the Jews, he had been only a secret disciple of our Lord. See <reference osisRef="Joh.19.38">Joh 19:38</reference>. <div eID="gen39693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39694" type="x-p"/> The apostle says, We have Boldness to enter into the holiest through his blood. Strange as it may appear, the death of Jesus is the grand cause of confidence and courage to a believing soul.
entries.c655492f8cb24ba382a9b04c4b18386090bf4adc: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen39694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39695" type="x-p"/> Beheld where he was laid - The courage and affection of these holy women cannot be too much admired. The strength of the Lord is perfected in weakness; for here a timid man, and a few weak women, acknowledge Jesus in death, when the strong and the mighty utterly forsook him. <div eID="gen39695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39696" type="x-p"/> Human strength and human weakness are only names in religion. The mightiest Man, in the hour of trial, can do nothing without the strength of God; and the weakest Woman can do all things, if Christ strengthen her. These truths are sufficiently exemplified in the case of Peter and all his brother disciples on the one hand; and Joseph of Arimathea and the two Marys on the other. And all this is recorded, equally to prevent both presumption and despair. Reader, let not these examples be produced before thee in vain.  <chapter eID="Mark.15"/> <div eID="gen39696" type="x-p"/>
