entries.8f553bf98dfb0900f616dc63b184d47e43eeea86:
Verse 25. And it was the third hour, etc. In Jn 19:14, it is said, "And it was the preparation of the Passover, and about the sixth hour," etc. Much difficulty has been felt in reconciling these passages; and infidels have usually adduced them to prove that the evangelists have contradicted themselves. In reconciling them the following remarks may perhaps make the matter clear.

(1.) The Jews divided both the night and the day into four equal parts of three hours each. Mt 14:25. The first division of the day commenced at six o'clock in the morning, and ended at nine; the second commenced at nine, and ended at twelve, etc. The third hour, mentioned by Mark, would therefore correspond with our nine o'clock; the sixth hour, mentioned by John, would correspond with our twelve, or noon.

(2.) Mark professes to give the time accurately; John does not. He says "it was about the sixth hour," without affirming that this was exactly the time.

(3.) A mistake in numbers is easily made; and if it should be admitted that such an error had crept into the text here, it would be nothing more than has occurred in many ancient writings. It has been proved, moreover, that it was common not to write the words indicating numbers at length, but to use letters. The Greeks designated numbers by the letters of the alphabet; and this mode of computation is found in ancient manuscripts, For example, the Cambridge Ms. of the New Testament has in this very place in Mark not the word third written at length, but the letter γ, Gamma, the usual notation for third. Now, it is well known that it would be easy to mistake this for the mark denoting six, . All error of this kind in an early MS might be extensively propagated, and might have led to the present reading of the text. Such an error is actually known to exist in the "Chronicon" of Paschal, where Otho is said to have reigned (six) months; whereas it is known that he reigned but three; and in this place therefore the γ, three, was mistaken for , six.

(4.) There is some external authority for reading "third" in Jn 19:14. The Cambridge MS has this reading. Nonnus, who lived in the fifth century, says that this was the true reading. (Wetstein.) Peter of Alexandria, in a fragment concerning the passover, as quoted by Usher, says, "It was the preparation of the passover, and about the third hour, as," he adds, "the most accurate copies of the Bible have it; and this was the handwriting of the Evangelist (John) which is kept, by the grace of God, in his most holy church at Ephesus." (Mill.) It is to be admitted, however, that no great reliance is to be placed on this account. That a mistake might have occurred in the early MSS. is not improbable. No man can prove that it did not so occur; and as long as this cannot be proved, the passages should not be adduced as conclusive proof of contradiction.

After all, perhaps the whole difficulty may be removed by the following statements:

(1.) Calvary was without the walls of Jerusalem. It was a considerable distance from the place where Jesus was tried and condemned. Some time--more or less--would be occupied in going there, and in the preparatory measures for crucifying him.

(2.) It is not necessary to understand Mark as saying that it was precisely nine o'clock, according to our expression. With the Jews, it was six until seven; it was the third hour until the fourth commenced; it was the ninth until it was the tenth. They included in the third hour the whole time from the third to the fourth. The same mode they adopted in regard to their days. Mt 12:40.

(3.) It is not unduly pressing the matter to suppose that Mark spoke of the time when the process for crucifixion commenced; i. e., when he was condemned; when they entered upon it; when they made the preparation. Between that and the time when he was taken out of Jerusalem to Mount Calvary, and when he was actually nailed to the tree, there is no improbability in supposing that there might have been an interval of more than an hour. Indeed, the presumption is, that considerably more time than that would elapse.

(4.) John does not profess, as has been remarked, to be strictly accurate. He says, "it was about the sixth hour," etc.

(5.) Now suppose that John meant to indicate the tune when he was actually suspended on the cross; that he spoke of the crucifixion denoting the act of suspension, as it struck him, and there is no difficulty. Any other two men--many witnesses might give just such an account now. One man would speak of the time when the process for an execution commenced, another perhaps of the very act of the execution, and would both speak of it in general terms, and say that a man was executed at such a time. And the circumstantial variation would prove that there was no collusion--no agreement to impose on a court--that they were honest witnesses. That is prosed here,

(6.) That this is the true account of the matter is clear from the evangelists themselves; and especially from Mark. The three first evangelists concur in stating that there was a remarkable darkness over the whole land from the sixth to the ninth hour, Mt 27:45; Mk 15:33; Lk 23:44. This fact would seem to indicate that the actual crucifixion continued only during that time--that he was, in fact, suspended at about the sixth hour, though the preparations for crucifying him had been going on (Mark) for two hours before. The fact, that Mark (Mk 15:33) mentions this darkness as commencing at the sixth and not at the third hour, is one of the circumstances undesignedly occurring that seems to signify that the crucifixion then had actually taken place--though the various arrangements for it (Mk 15:26) had been going on from the third hour.

One thing is conclusively proved by this, that the evangelists did not conspire together to impose on the world. They are independent witnesses; and they were honest men. And the circumstance adverted to here is one that is allowed to be of great value in testimony in courts of justice--circumstantial variation with essential agreement.

entries.5f6e39d8213613be35f86f4a676ddb649e586c3b:
Verse 43. Joseph--an honourable counsellor. A distinguished man, who probably held a high office among the Jews, as one of their great council or a Jewish senator. The word honourable here is not a mere title of office, but is given in reference to his personal character, as being a man of integrity and blameless life.

Waited for the kingdom of God. Waited for, or expected, the coming of the Messiah. But this expression means more than an indefinite expectation that the Messiah would come, for all the Jews expected that. It implies that he believed Jesus to be the Messiah, and that he had waited for him to build up the kingdom of God; and this agrees with what John says, Jn 19:38 that he was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews. He had retained his secret belief in the hope that Jesus would be proclaimed and treated as the Messiah, and then he probably proposed openly to acknowledge his attachment to him. But God called him to a public profession of attachment in a different manner, and gave this distinguished man grace to evince it. So men often delay a profession of attachment to Christ. They cherish a secret love; they indulge a hope in the mercy of God; but they conceal it for fear of man. Whereas God requires that the attachment should be made known. "He that is ashamed of me," said the Saviour, "and of my words before men, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed when he shall come in the glory of his Father and of the holy angels." Those who love the Saviour have no right to hide their light under a bushel. As soon as they have evidence, satisfactory to their own mind, that they are Christians, or have a prevalent belief, after faithful examination, that they truly love God, and depend on the Lord Jesus for salvation, so soon are they bound to profess Christ before men. This is the command of God, and this is the way of peace. None have the prospect of comfort in religion, who do not have respect to all of the commandments of God.

Went in boldly unto Pilate. God had raised up this distinguished counsellor and secret disciple for a special and most important vocation. The disciples of Jesus had fled; and if they had not, they had no influence with Pilate. Unless there had been a special application to Pilate in behalf of Jesus, his body would have been buried that night in the common grave with the malefactors: for it was a law of the Jews that the body of an executed man should not remain on the cross on the sabbath. At this critical juncture, God called forward this secret disciple--this friend of Jesus, though unknown as such to the world, and gave him confidence; he dared to express sympathy for the Saviour; he went in boldly, and begged the body of Jesus. It needed no small measure of courage to do this. Jesus had just been condemned, mocked, spit on, crucified--the death of a slave, or the most guilty wretch. To avow attachment for him now was proof of sincere affection; and the Holy Spirit has thought this worthy of special notice; and has set down this bold attachment of a senator for Jesus, for our imitation.

Craved the body. Begged, or asked.

entries.ce967a230fc40b0cddfa2fb862f85dd918f9f54e: Verse 44. And Pilate marvelled if, etc. Wondered if he was dead; or wondered that he was so soon dead. entries.1ae5bd730a474ff0dc11a94dd19db674bb3b6109: Verse 45. When he knew it of the centurion. Being informed by the centurion of the fact that he was dead. The centurion had charge of the soldiers who watched him, and could therefore give correct information.
entries.af405247928f22ca138a876f106301cea39dfdb2: Verse 47. Beheld where he was laid. The affection of these pious females never forsook them, in all the trials and sufferings of their Lord. With true love they followed him to the cross; they came as near to him as they were permitted to come, in his last moments; they followed him when taken down and laid in the tomb. The strong, the mighty, the youthful, had fled; but female love never forsook him, even in his deepest humiliation. This is the nature of true love. It is strongest in such scenes. While professed attachment will abound in prosperity, and live most in sunshine, it is only genuine love that will go into the dark shades of adversity, and flourish there. In scenes of poverty, want, affliction, and death, it shows its genuineness. That which lives there is genuine; that which turns away from such scenes is spurious.

entries.62ab0f2a2f3271198efcf6a7260693f33201fa77: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.15.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.15.25" sID="gen102904" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.25">Mark 15:25</reference></hi> <hi type="italic">And it was the third hour. </hi>This appears not to agree well with the testimony of the Evangelist John; for he relates that Christ was condemned <hi type="italic">about the sixth hour, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.14">14:14</reference>.) But if we consider—what is evident from other passages—that the day was divided into four parts, and that each of the parts took its name from the first hour of its commencement, the solution will not be difficult. The whole time, from sunrise to the second part of the day, they called <hi type="italic">the first </hi>hour. The second part, which lasted till noon, was called by them the <hi type="italic">third </hi>hour. The <hi type="italic">sixth </hi>hour commenced at noon, and lasted till three or four o’clock in the afternoon. Thus, when the Jews saw that Pilate was wearing out the time, and that the hour of noon was approaching, John <hi type="italic">says </hi>that <hi type="italic">they cried out </hi>the more vehemently, that the whole day might not be allowed to pass without something being done, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.15">14:15</reference>.) But this is not inconsistent with the assertion, that our Lord was crucified about the close of <hi type="italic">the third hour; </hi>for it is plain enough, that no sooner was he hastily condemned, than he was immediately executed; so eager was the desire of the Jews to put him to death. Mark therefore means not the beginning, but the close, of the third hour; and it is highly probable that Christ did not hang on the cross longer than three hours.<div eID="gen102905" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.15.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102904" osisID="Mark.15.25" type="section"/>
entries.bbd69adbdf59ed750e044ab01f9dff501c2f5ff4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.15.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.15.36" sID="gen102994" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.36">Mark 15:36</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Saying, Let him alone, let us see if Elijah will come to save him. Mark </hi>relates these words as having been spoken by the soldier, while holding out the vinegar; but Matthew tells us that others used the same language. There is no inconsistency here, however; for it is probable that the jeering was begun by one person, but was eagerly seized by others, and loudly uttered by the multitude. The phrase, <hi type="italic">let him alone, </hi>appears to have implied not restraint, but ridicule; accordingly, the person who first mocked Christ, ironically addressing his companions, says, <hi type="italic">Let us see if Elijah will come. </hi>Others quickly followed, and every one sung the same song to his next neighbor, as usually happens with men who are agreed about any course. Nor is it of any importance to inquire if it was in the singular or plural number; for in either case the meaning is the same, the word being used in place of an interjection, as if they had said, <hi type="italic">Hush! Hush!</hi><div eID="gen102995" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.15.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102994" osisID="Mark.15.36" type="section"/>
entries.478f364d5d07ee1768dca7919f19d0911bc5173e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.15.43" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.15.43" sID="gen103047" type="section"/> <div sID="gen103048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.43">Mark 15:43</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.51">Luke 23:51</reference>.</hi> Who also himself was waiting for the kingdom of God. The highest commendation bestowed on Joseph is, that he waited for the kingdom of God. He is likewise praised, no doubt, for righteousness, but this waiting for the kingdom of God was the root and source of his righteousness. By the kingdom of God, we must understand the renovation promised through Christ; for the perfection of order which, the prophets had every where promised, would exist at the coming of Christ, cannot exist, unless God assembles under his government those men who had gone astray. It is therefore pointed out in commendation of Joseph’s piety, that, during the disorder which then prevailed, he cherished the hope of that redemption which God had promised. Hence, too, arises the fear of God, and the desire of holiness and uprightness; for it is impossible for any one to dedicated himself to God, unless he expects that God will be his deliverer.<div eID="gen103048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103049" type="x-p"/>Yet let us observe, that while salvation through Christ was promised indiscriminately to all the Jews, and while the promise of it was common to them all, it is only of a very few that the Holy Spirit testifies what we are here told of Joseph. Hence it is evident, that nearly the whole of the people had buried in base forgetfulness the inestimable grace of God. All of them, indeed, had on their lips the language of boasting in reference to the coming of Christ, which was approaching; but few had the covenant of God fixed in their minds, so as to rise by faith to spiritual renovation. That was indeed an awful insensibility; and therefore we need not wonder if pure religion fell into decay, when the faith of salvation was extinguished. Would to God that a similar corruption did not prevail in this unhappy age! Christ once appeared as a Redeemer to the Jews and to the whole world, as had been declared in the predictions of the prophets. He set up <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God, </hi>by restoring affairs from confusion and disorder to a regular and proper condition. He has assigned to us a period of warfare, to exercise our patience till he come again from heaven to complete his reign which he has commenced. How many are there who aspire to this hope, even in a moderate degree? Do not almost all cleave to the earth, as if there had been no promise of a resurrection? But while the greater part of men, forgetful of their end, fall off on all sides, let us remember that it is a virtue peculiar to believers, to <hi type="italic">seek the things which are above,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.3.1">Colossians 3:1</reference>;) and especially since the grace of God has shone upon us through the Gospel,<div eID="gen103049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen103050" type="x-p"/>teaching us, that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, justly, and piously, in the present world, looking for the blessed hope and manifestation of the glory of the great God,<lb/> (<reference osisRef="">Titus 2:11-13</reference>.)<div eID="gen103050" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.15.43" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen103047" osisID="Mark.15.43" type="section"/>

In our Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2.3.4, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> We have compared, and considered them all, and shall thither refer the <ns0:hi>Reader.</ns0:hi> Only observing, 1. <ns0:hi>How much more favour</ns0:hi> Christ found from a <ns0:hi>Gentile Heathen,</ns0:hi> than from the <ns0:hi>Iewish High Priest,</ns0:hi> and not Favour only, but <ns0:hi>Iustice</ns0:hi> also. 2. <ns0:hi>Hour close our Saviour kept upon his Guard,</ns0:hi> not accusing himself. 3. <ns0:hi>The horrible de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bauchery of these Priests, that they would prefer a Murderer, and Seditious Person, before a most innocent Person.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>The weakness of a corrupt heart, to resist an ordinary Temptation. Pilate</ns0:hi> was convinced the Prosecution was Malicious, that there was no guilt in Christ; yet he must content the People, and is basely afraid of their misrepresenting him to the <ns0:hi>Roman Emperour.</ns0:hi> 5. <ns0:hi>That the point upon which Christ was Condemned, was his maintaining his spiritual Kingdom, in, and over his Church,</ns0:hi> for he expresly disclaimed any claim to any <ns0:hi>earthly Kingdom,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> as the other Evangelists tell us. 6. <ns0:hi>How punctually</ns0:hi> the words of Christ are, by the Providence of God fulfilled, we have now heard how Christ was delivered to the Gentiles, by them <ns0:hi>mocked, scourged, spit upon,</ns0:hi> and now going to be killed. 7. <ns0:hi>How Christ hath made all our bitter Waters sweet?</ns0:hi> Sanctifying every cross to us, and taking the curse out of it. He was reviled<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> imprisoned, mocked, scourged, spit upon, and last of all killed; he hath tasted of all these bitter Watters, and by that tast they are made wholesome, and medicinal for us, and he hath learned us, that there is no ignominy, shame, and contempt, no indignity, and <ns0:hi>species</ns0:hi> of suffering for his sake, in which we may not boast and Glory, as being thereby made conformable to the sufferings, and Death of Christ. And if we suffer with him, we shall be glorified together.</ns0:note>

John 19. <ns0:hi>from v.</ns0:hi> 17. <ns0:hi>to v.</ns0:hi> 30.</ns0:note> they compel one Simon a Cyrenian, who passed by, coming out of the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to bear his cross.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And they bring him unto the place Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, the place of a scull.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And they gave him to drink, wine mingled with myrrhe: but he received <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And when they had crucified him, they <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 22.18. John 19.23.</ns0:note> part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed his garments, casting lots upon them, what every man should take.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>See</ns0:hi> Matth. 27.45. Luke 23.44. John 19.14.</ns0:note> it was the third hour, and they cruci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 27.37. John 19.19.</ns0:note> the superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 27.38.</ns0:note> with him they crucifie two thieves; the one on his right hand, and the other on his left.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And the scripture was fulfilled, which saith, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isaiah 53.12. Luke 22.37.</ns0:note> And he was numbred with the transgressors.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal 22.7.</ns0:note> they that passed by, railed on him, wag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ging their heads, and saying, Ah, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 14.58.</ns0:note> thou that destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est the temple, and buildest <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> in three days,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Save thy self, and come down from the cross.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 Likewise also the chief priests mocking, said among themselves, with the scribes, He saved others, himself he cannot save.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 Let Christ the king of Israel descend now from the cross, that we may see, and believe. And they that were crucified with him; reviled him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 27.45.</ns0:note> when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land, until the ninth hour.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 22.1. Matth. 27.46.</ns0:note> Eloi, Eloi, lame sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And some of them that stood by, when they heard <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> said, Behold, he calleth Elias.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">John 19.29.</ns0:note> one ran, and filled a spunge full of vine<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gar, and put <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> on a reed, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 69.21.</ns0:note> gave him to drink, saying, Let alone, let us see whether Elias will come to take him down.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 27.50<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> John 19.30</ns0:note> And Jesus cryed with a loud voice, and gave up the ghost.<ns0:note place="bottom">To make this History compleat, all the other Evangelists must be consulted, and compared with <ns0:hi>Mark,</ns0:hi> who omitteth many con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siderable passages recorded by them, we have done it in our Notes on <ns0:hi>Math.</ns0:hi> 27.32, 33, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> to which I refer the <ns0:hi>Reader,</ns0:hi> both for the understanding the several passages of this Relation, and recon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciling any small differences betwixt the Relations of the several Evangelists. It is the observation of some, that when in Scripture the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> is made known by the <ns0:hi>Son,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Sons,</ns0:hi> it signifieth some more eminency in the Sons, then in the Father. Many think that this <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> was a <ns0:hi>Pagan,</ns0:hi> tho it be not certain, yet it is not impro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable, that this <ns0:hi>Alexander</ns0:hi> was the same who is mentioned, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 19.33. persecuted there by the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rufus</ns0:hi> he whom<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> saluteth <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 16.13. calling him <ns0:hi>chosen in the Lord.</ns0:hi> They say they were both at <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> where they judge St. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> was when he wrote this History, and that <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> mentioneth them, as those who could attest the truth of this part of the History. The <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> bare Christ's Cross, (or one end of it,) there is all we read of him. The Sons believe on him, who died upon it. So free is Divine Grace, fixing where it pleaseth. Concerning the Wine mingled <ns0:hi>with Myrrhe,</ns0:hi> we spake in our Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27. Some think our Saviours friends gave it him, to refresh him: But it is most prob<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ble it was given him to entoxicate him, that he might be less sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sible of the pain he should endure upon the Cross; whatsoever they intended, our Saviour refused it, having <ns0:hi>Wine</ns0:hi> to uphold him, which they knew not of. For other things relating to this Story, see the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth</ns0:hi> 27.32.33.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:291" />38 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 23 47, 48, 49.</ns0:note> And the vail of the temple was rent in twain, from the top to the bottom.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And when the centurion which stood over a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst him, saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 There were also women looking on afar off: among whom was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less, and of Joses, and Salome.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 Who also when he was <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 3.3.</ns0:note> in Galilee, followed him, and ministred unto him; and many other women which came up with him unto Jerusalem.<ns0:note place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Prodigies</ns0:hi> happening upon the Death of our Saviour, and the passages happening betwixt the time of his expiration, and his Burial, are more largely reported by the other Evangelists then by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi>; we have put them all together, and considered the passages relating to them in our Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 51.52.53. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>

               <ns0:p n="42">42 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 23.50. John 19.38.</ns0:note> And now when the even was come, (because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath:)</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 Joseph of Arimathea, an honourable coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 And Pilate marvelled if he were already dead: and calling unto him the centurion, he asked him Whether he had been any while dead.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 And when he knew <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> of the centurion, he gave the body to Joseph.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 And he bought fine linnen, and took him down, and wrapped him in the linnen, and laid him in a se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pulchre which was hewen out of a rock, and rolled a stone unto the door of the sepulchre.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 And Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of Joses, beheld where he was laid.<ns0:note place="bottom">The circumstances of our Saviours honourable burial as related by this, and the other <ns0:hi>Evangelists,</ns0:hi> are gathered together, and opened in our <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> 27. from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 57. to 66.</ns0:note>
